name: Block a deploy when pages go noindex with an SEO smoke test and Slack

parameters.content:
## Block a deploy that makes your site invisible

The expensive SEO incidents are not slow declines. They are a staging setting reaching production and every page quietly telling search engines not to index it. Nothing looks broken; the graph falls three weeks later. This is a webhook your pipeline calls after it ships, and it answers with a status code so the pipeline can stop the release.

### How it works

**`Fetch Each Page`** asks without following redirects. HTTP Request v4 follows them unless it is explicitly told not to, and a URL that used to be a page and now 301s elsewhere is exactly the regression worth catching.

**`Check Every Page`** reads `X-Robots-Tag` **and** the robots meta tag. The header is invisible to an HTML parser and is the only way to say noindex on a PDF or a feed - `community.n8n.io/search` answers 200 with `x-robots-tag: noindex`. It carries directives rather than a switch, so the value is read, not its presence.

**`Read robots.txt`** is separate because `Disallow: /` blocks a whole site and appears on no page.

A 401 or 403 is a warning, not a failure. A fresh environment behind basic auth answers exactly like a broken page, and a check that cries wolf gets deleted from the pipeline.

### Setup

1. Publish the workflow and POST to the Production URL from your pipeline: `{"urls": ["https://you.com/", "https://you.com/pricing"], "label": "deploy abc123"}`.

2. With no body it falls back to the list in **Settings**, so it can be run by hand.

3. A Slack credential. Point `slack_channel` at wherever deploys are announced.

4. A failure answers **HTTP 500**, so `curl --fail` in your pipeline is enough to stop the release.

## 1. Your pipeline calls it
POST the URLs you just deployed. With no body it falls back to the Settings list, so it runs by hand too.

## 2. Ask, without following
HTTP Request v4 follows redirects unless told not to. A page that now 301s elsewhere is the regression worth catching, and by default it is invisible.

## 3. The two site-wide files
`Disallow: /` blocks everything and appears on no page. A missing sitemap entry is only ever a warning.

## 4. Blocker or warning
A 401 or 403 is a warning: a fresh environment behind basic auth answers exactly like a broken page.

## 5. Say what broke
Two messages, because a blocked deploy and a deploy that went out with warnings are read by different people in a different mood.

## 6. Answer the pipeline
A failure answers HTTP 500, so `curl --fail` is enough to stop the release. Nothing else is needed on the pipeline side.

## Keep the failure list short

Everything here fails a deploy. Anything you would not roll back for belongs in `warn`, not `fail` - a gate that fires on things nobody acts on is a gate somebody removes.
